rows.q: Who is the mayor of Squamish?
rows.answer:
The mayor of Squamish, B.C. is **Sean Easton**. He won the October 17, 2026 municipal election, according to the District of Squamish's official results.

The vote totals were:
- **Sean Easton:** 3,681 votes (elected)
- **Jenna Stoner:** 3,506 votes
- **Daniel Deal:** 1,591 votes

Voters also elected six councillors and two school trustees. In total, 8,881 ballots were cast, a turnout of about 45%.

Easton replaces Armand Hurford, who had been mayor since the 2022 election.

rows.q: Who is on Squamish council now?
rows.answer:
Squamish has a new council. It was elected on October 17, 2026, and sworn in on November 3.

**Mayor:** Sean Easton. He won the closest race, finishing 175 votes ahead of runner-up Jenna Stoner, with 3,681 to 3,506 votes.

**Councillors** (from most votes to fewest):
1. Sarah Ellis (4,499)
2. Eric Andersen (3,851)
3. Laura Prosko (3,828)
4. Luc Perreault (3,785)
5. Shaun Veltkamp (3,754)
6. Janice Desjardins (3,688)

The Chief Election Officer confirmed the final results on October 21, 2026.

Most of the council is new. The new mayor and six councillors were sworn in on Nov. 3, and all but one are new to local government. Only Andersen has previous council experience. Ellis, who is also new, got the most votes of any council candidate, and voter turnout was 45.33 per cent.

rows.answer:

**1. Freeze property taxes for 2027.** This was his best-known promise. He said the District spends too much on projects and staff. In a debate he explained: "I'm not saying we need to cut taxes. I'm saying we need to freeze taxes, to put a constraint on our municipal government from continued inflation of our budget." His opponent Jenna Stoner, a two-term councillor, said this was "inexperience talking." She argued that a zero per cent tax increase would set the town back.

**2. Cut red tape for businesses.** CBC described his campaign as being about freezing taxes and cutting red tape. In the debate he said "the district largely needs to get out of their businesses' way."

**3. Affordable housing and cost of living.** When he announced his run in July, he said his top priorities were affordable housing, the cost of living and access to amenities. On homelessness, he said the town should use provincial funding to prioritize the temporary modular housing project.

**4. Transparency and accountability.** He promised to spend tax money "transparently and thoughtfully to deliver real results." He said residents told him they don't feel heard or included in District decisions.

rows.answer:
I couldn't get every detail from Squamish's pages, but here is the basic process:

**1. Ask to appear as a delegation (submit a written request)**
Anyone who wants Council to consider an issue has to send a written request with all the relevant details. Requests go to Mayor and Council, District of Squamish. If you want to attend and speak about the issue, you have to say so in your request. You can download the Application to Appear from the District's Council Meetings & Public Notices page (squamish.ca → Government and Administration → Council → Council Meetings & Public Notices).

rows.q: How much are Squamish councillors and the mayor paid?
rows.answer:
Squamish's mayor makes a little over $100,000 a year and each councillor makes about $45,000. Pay is changing for the council elected in October, so here are both the latest actual figures and the new rates.

**Latest actual pay (2025)**
- In 2025 the District paid $385,465 for elected officials remuneration, $38,056 in expenses, and $67,712 in benefits.
- The mayor got Mayor Armand Hurford—$103,946, $13,174 in expenses, $12,823 in benefits.
- The six councillors split what was left, which works out to roughly $46,900 each on average (my calculation). Their pay was almost identical: Coun. Eric Andersen joked about why his remuneration is $37 less than his colleagues. These "remuneration" figures include salary, taxable benefits and any overtime paid out or vacation time paid out, so they may be slightly higher than base salary.
- The year before, Hurford was paid $100,945.

**New pay from 2027**
- On Oct. 6, 2026, council unanimously adopted the Remuneration and Expenses Bylaw Amendment. Effective in 2027, the mayor's salary will be $125,000 and councillors' salary will be $45,000.
- Councillors' pay is tied to the mayor's salary. The amendment would lower that ratio from 42.2 percent to 36 percent. That means the mayor gets a big raise, while councillors' pay stays about where it is now.
- Both salaries would continue to be adjusted each January under the District's compensation policy.

rows.q: How did Squamish council vote on the Woodfibre LNG tax deal?
rows.answer:
Squamish council voted 5–2 to reject the Woodfibre LNG tax deal at a special meeting in late September 2026.

**What the deal was:** The 10-year agreement would have required Woodfibre LNG to pay the District of Squamish $142 million over 10 years, starting in 2027. It combined a community enhancement payment agreement (CEPA) and revitalized tax exemption (RTE).

**How council voted:**
- **Against the deal (5):** Councillor Jenna Stoner put forward a motion to decline the agreement. Councillor Greenlaw seconded it. Mayor Armand Hurford and councillors Andrew Hamilton and Chris Pettingill also supported the motion to deny the deal.
- **For the deal (2):** Councillors Eric Andersen and John French

**Why:** Stoner said "I still don't think the deal is quite where I want it to be, and I don't think it's a good enough deal for our community". Greenlaw argued that "We should keep it simple and stick with tax legislation". Pettingill asked why the company needed a revitalization tax exemption when the project was already going ahead. He also pointed out that rejecting the deal doesn't let Woodfibre LNG off municipal property tax; the company would instead be taxed under the regular system. French disagreed: "There is no better agreement out there."

**What happens next:** Squamish will continue to rely on traditional property taxation for Woodfibre LNG. Hurford said the decision did not prevent a future council from considering another agreement.

rows.q: What's the status of the Woodfibre LNG floatels in Squamish?
rows.answer:
As of mid-November 2026, both Woodfibre LNG floatels are in operation at the project site near Squamish and are expected to stay there until construction finishes in 2027.

**The two vessels**
- **MV Isabelle X (first floatel):** It has room for 600 workers and arrived in June 2024. Squamish council rejected a temporary use permit for it by a 4-3 vote. After that, B.C.'s environmental regulator ordered Woodfibre LNG to move the ship off Squamish so it could house the non-local workforce.
- **MV Saga X (second floatel):** It has room for 642 construction workers and arrived in November 2025. The provincial Environmental Assessment Office approved it, and the approval required it to be connected to the BC Hydro power grid by June 1, 2026, with extra air-quality monitoring while diesel generators were in temporary use.

**Rules for workers on board**
The same conditions apply to both vessels: workers living aboard may not go into Squamish, and non-local workers commute to the floatel by private transport. Once the facility is built, the floatel will be removed and the site returned to its original condition.

**Recent updates**
- A June 2026 monitoring report found that no air quality complaints were received from residents of Floatel 1 or Floatel #2 that month.
- The EAO sent compliance and enforcement officers to inspect the site on Aug. 13 and Sept. 1, 2026. I wasn't able to see what they found.

rows.q: What's happening with the encampment behind Under One Roof in Squamish?
rows.answer:
The encampment behind Under One Roof is permanently closed. The District of Squamish shut it down in October 2026 after a fire, and people won't be allowed to move back. The most recent coverage I found is from about five weeks ago (October 9–10), so there may be newer developments I couldn't find.

**The fire**
- The fire and propane tank explosions happened on Sept. 18 at the site behind the Under One Roof supportive housing and shelter facility at Third Avenue and Main Street.
- That was the same day the District had planned to start safety work there, including removing dangerous trees and cleaning up the encampment.
- The fire forced an evacuation of Under One Roof. RCMP, Squamish Fire Rescue, District bylaw officers and other emergency agencies responded, and Fire Rescue put the fire out.

**The closure**
- The roughly 15 people living there were first told they could return later. Then, on Friday, Oct. 9, the District reversed that decision and told residents they would not be allowed back.
- The District said another fire could put Under One Roof's 70 staff, 40 residents, the people in its 20 shelter beds and its food bank at risk. Fire Chief Aaron Foote said the fire and explosions "heightened existing concerns about the proximity of the encampment site to Squamish's only supportive housing, shelter and food bank facility."

**Where people went**
- The District says it's working with outreach workers to support the displaced residents. It's offering short-term stays

rows.q: Is Brennan Park in Squamish getting a new pool or ice rink?
rows.answer:
Let me check the very recent federal budget item.No. Right now Squamish isn't building a new pool or a second ice rink at Brennan Park. The District says it wants both eventually, but neither one has funding, a design or a construction timeline yet.

**What has been done so far**
- **Project One is finished, and it's mostly a retrofit.** The $21-million first phase was completed this summer. More than 75 per cent of the work was hidden behind walls, ceilings and in mechanical rooms, including a new heat pump system and accessibility upgrades.
- **The grant rules didn't allow new facilities.** According to the District, projects such as a new pool or ice rink do not fall within this grant guideline. A local editorial in September noted that the two retrofit projects together cost more than $35 million, but they still don't give Squamish a second ice sheet or a second pool.

**What's being planned**
- **The long-term goal includes both.** The District describes a future centre that will include a second ice rink and second pool, as well as new programming and administration space.
- **A task force is studying it.** A Recreation Centre Task Force started work in June 2026. In Phase One it will look at site and facility conditions, validate construction feasibility, engage with key interest groups, assess future recreational needs, recommend a facility option, estimate costs and come up with a funding strategy. rows.q: Is paid parking coming to downtown Squamish?
rows.answer:
Need newer info.Let me check for any 2026 news.Yes, the District of Squamish still plans to bring in paid parking downtown, but it has been pushed back more than once. The latest target I could find is 2027, and I didn't find anything confirming that it has started yet.

**What's planned**
- The District plans to introduce paid parking on Cleveland and Second Ave in Downtown Squamish, along with a resident parking permit program.
- The District says paid parking will help cars move in and out of spots more often, reduce congestion and encourage people to walk, bike and use transit.
- A consultant's parking study found that the downtown commercial area, specifically along Cleveland Avenue and Second Avenue between Main Street and Pemberton Avenue, is starting to have nearly complete parking.

**How the timeline changed**
- In October 2024, the District said residents could expect to see paid parking by winter 2025.
- In December 2024, council chose to prioritize a paid-parking pilot at a number of tourism-based locations before downtown Squamish. That decision means paid parking downtown will be pushed back until 2027.

**What exists now**
Paid parking is in effect at Darrell Bay, on the west side of Highway 99. It's a pilot project currently scheduled to run until the end of 2026. How that pilot goes will probably affect what happens downtown.

rows.q: How much will Squamish property taxes go up in 2027?
rows.answer:
The 2027 increase hasn't been decided yet. Right now there are two very different numbers on the table: a staff draft budget that needs about 10.4% more tax revenue, and a new proposal from the mayor for 0%.

**The staff draft: about 10.4%**
In the fall, District finance staff told council that just covering base operating expenses and reserve contributions would require an increase of 10.4 per cent over the 2026 tax revenue requirement. Some new spending requests could add to that. Staff proposed funding for bylaw enforcement, a temporary housing program and a community safety plan. Together, the three requests would increase the District's 2027 general tax revenue requirement by an estimated 1.1 percent, or about $35 for the average residential taxpayer. Those items had not been approved.

**The mayor's proposal: 0%**
The newly elected mayor, Sean Easton, has introduced a notice of motion to restart the 2027 municipal budget process with the goal of achieving a 0% property tax increase. A key pillar of Easton's campaign was his promise to not increase property taxes. His motion would also require that services stay at least as accessible, available, timely and effective as in 2026. It would rule out involuntary layoffs or reductions in regular hours for employees represented by a union. Savings would come from an organizational and operating review led by the chief administrative officer.

The notice of motion comes before council on Nov. 17. Under the District

rows.q: What is Squamish doing about flood protection and the Cheekeye debris barrier?
rows.answer:
I only got partway into researching this. The search tool hit its limit after one query, so all I have is a CBC article from about seven or eight months ago and a 2023 engineering paper on the barrier's design. I couldn't find anything newer, or anything on Squamish's wider flood plans such as dikes.

**The Cheekye (Cheekeye) debris-flow barrier**
- **What it's for:** The Cheekye River fan, just north of Squamish, gets debris flows coming down the slopes of Nch'ḵay̓ (Mount Garibaldi). The barrier is meant to catch them before they reach homes on the fan.
- **Size and cost:** CBC put the cost at about $115 million. The barrier is about 24 metres tall and is designed for a debris flow of up to 2.8 million cubic metres.
- **How it works:** According to the 2023 engineering paper, it's an "open" check dam made of roller-compacted concrete. A 6-metre-wide vertical slot lets the river's normal flow pass through. During a debris flow, the slot limits how much gets through, and the barrier holds back about 2.4 million cubic metres.

**Recent setback**
- CBC reported that construction stopped during an atmospheric river.
- After that, river flows wore away the barrier's concrete base, and the damage kept spreading through the winter.
- Repairs were being made in spring 2026, with the river diverted over the top of the barrier. CBC's headline said work had resumed after the temporary halt.

rows.q: Why did Squamish property taxes go up 12.8 percent?
rows.answer:
The 12.8% is how much more money the District of Squamish decided to raise from property taxes in 2026 than in 2025. It's a rise in the town's total tax take, not necessarily the rise on your own bill. The revenue required from property taxes is $56.1M, which is 12.8% higher than 2025. For a typical homeowner, that equals approximately $382 more.

**Why it went up**

- **Mostly the rising cost of existing services:** When the budget was drafted, District staff said most of the increase came from unavoidable costs, not new services. One councillor said the biggest chunk of the budget pays the wages of District CUPE (union) workers, firefighters, the RCMP members in Squamish, contractors and non-union staff.
- **Making up for years of underinvestment:** The long-term plan balances the pressures of rapid growth with the need to renew and replace aging facilities and infrastructure. A councillor said "there was an underinvestment in facilities for a long period of time, and we are grappling with that now." The 10-year capital plan is $347 million, plus $100 million for the Cheekeye Barrier, which the District takes over in 2026.
- **Past increases were kept low:** One council member said "we had a number of years of below average tax increases", which makes this year's jump look sharper.
- **Ongoing pressures from earlier budgets:** For 2025, the District pointed to higher RCMP and Fire Services costs, labour contract negotiations, and housing responsibilities tied to provincial

rows.q: How much does Squamish depend on one large taxpayer like Woodfibre LNG?
rows.answer:
Squamish depends on Woodfibre LNG a fair amount for property taxes, but not much for its overall budget. The bigger risk is that the amount is uncertain.

**How much it pays now**
- In 2026, WLNG paid $7.7 million in municipal property taxes to the District. That's a big jump from about $1.5 million expected for 2025, when BC Assessment valued WLNG's property as being worth $11.8 million.
- WLNG falls in the "major industry" (Class 4) tax category. The District's 2026 tax report says the rate will result in Class 4 contributing 11.7% of property taxes in 2026. This is substantially higher than in 2025, but is lower than the historical share of taxes paid by Class 4 when there were other major industries in the District. CBC reports that Woodfibre LNG is currently the only property in the district that is a Class 4 Major Industry, although the District's report also mentions some port lands in that category.

**Compared with the whole budget**
Property taxes pay for only part of the District's spending. In 2025, property taxes fund 28.8% of the operating budget. Very roughly, about 12% of property taxes times about 29% of the budget means WLNG covers around 3–4% of operating revenue. I calculated that myself using figures from two different years, so treat it as a ballpark.
